speechtext: The house proceeded to consideration of amendments made by the senate to Bill No. 142, to amend the Income War Tax Act.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS-CONTROL OF THE COMMONS OVER FINANCIAL MEASURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the amendments made by the senate to this bill are, in my opinion, far beyond ordinary modifications, as they alter periods during which certain income taxes shall be levied. They are not in the nature of fees or penalties imposed to punish certain offences, which this house sometimes accepts under protest. There was in the bill, as passed by this house, a clause providing that all its sections, except 16 and 17, shall be applicable to the income of the year 1938. The senate's amendment provides that section 6 shall be applicable to the income of the year 1939. This amendment changes the financial scheme submitted by the government and affects the balance of ways and means needed for the service of the year.
The action taken by the senate is inconsistent, I believe, with the undeniable control exercised by the elected representatives of the people over taxation and all financial measures.
The privilege of the House of Commons in this regard is based upon the fact that the house is composed of popularly elected members.
As Redlich, volume III, pages 119-120, says:
All taxes, duties and grants of money, and all measures imposing financial burdens on the people are matters within the sole jurisdiction of the House of Commons. Closely connected with the first of the Commons' rights in money matters is a second, inseparable from it and equally fundamental. They are entitled to order and dispose how the national revenue, whether permanent or annually granted, is to be spent, and to do so in the greatest detail.
Both income and expenditure are therefore completely and exclusively in the hands of the House of Commons.
The House of Commons, adhering to the British North America Act and the fundamental principles of responsible government; cannot renounce its inalienable right to initiate and regulate taxation, and it has never acknowledged the right of the senate to pass legislation imposing a charge upon the people.
Were the session not so near prorogation we should certainly refuse to accept this amendment; but a conference with the upper house for the discussion of this important question would last several days. It is hoped, however, that the senate will not persist in future in a course which we deem contrary to the principles of parliamentary practice and

which may lead to constitutional conflicts. The motion to concur in the amendment, with this reservation, will be .made by the Minister of National Revenue.

By the amendment which passed this house to the Income War Tax Act, only one year's interest on succession duties is allowed from any one year's income-that is, the interest accruing during that very year. By the act which passed this house the amendment related to the income of the year 1938 and subsequent years. By the senate amendment the retroactive feature is eliminated and the amendment relates only to the income of 1939 and succeeding years. There is, of course, something to be said for the amendment, on the merits. Oninions might differ. 
I believe that in this house the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Stewart) expressed very strongly the opinion that our amendment to the Income War Tax Act was not just, was not right; and I expressed the contrary opinion, or at least the opinion that it was inline with our usual amendments to the Income War Tax Act: they relate to the income tax returns which are being made, during spring and early summer, for the previous year. However, I can understand that on the justice and the merits of the case there might be a strong contrary view, and the government have decided that they do not particularly object to the merit of the senate amendment. It is, however, an infringement of the privileges of this house to make such an amendment in the senate.
The hon. gentleman said that -we were departing entirely from precedent. On certain rare occasions the House of Commons has done just what we are doing at the moment. We have asserted our position, affirmed our privileges and declined expressly to waive any of them, and had an entry to that effect made in the journals of the house. Nevertheless have accepted the amendment, and I think that that is the reasonable course to take in the circumstances. If there is at any time the slightest disposition in the other chamber to continue with this, undoubtedly we shall have to make an issue of it.

I do not think it is a question of discussing the merits or demerits of the amendment which has been made. To my mind, and I speak entirely as a layman, the question involves the privileges of this chamber, and the fundamental privilege of this chamber is that it shall have unchallenged control of the pursestrings, if I may put it that way. The long history of the development of our parliamentary institutions has been a struggle by the commons for the control of taxation and the expenditure of revenue; and in spite of the fact that the motion which has been moved to concur in the senate amendment is couched

Income War Tax
in very careful language, and sets out the privileges of this house in this regard, I think that it is unwise for this House of Commons to accept that motion, even in the form in which it is made. The time has long since passed when this parliament should have modified the powers of the other chamber. Nearly thirty years ago the British parliament made the House of Commons supreme over the House of Lords, and our position in this parliament is similar to the position of the British House of Commons before the passage of the Parliament Act in 1911. It seems to me that we should not concur in any manner in the action of the senate, that we should affirm our right in the proper way, which is to refuse to admit that the other chamber has any right whatsoever to interfere with a decision of this house regarding a matter of taxation and of revenue. In effect, although the motion to concur is carefully phrased, we are allowing a precedent to be made. We are objecting to it; nevertheless the precedent is there-

speechtext:
Perhaps I might explain the situation with regard to this difference of opinion between the senate and this house touching the rights of the senate on bills relating to money matters or to taxation. It is a long-standing conflict in this country, and the proposal for a conference might be stronger if we were not fully aware of the views of the senate-what they are and what they have been-and of our own views as well. Obviously there will have to be a settlement of this conflict some day. I would refer hon. members to page 172 of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, citations 582, 583 and 584, wherein they will see that the senate on one occasion went to the extent of asking the 71492-305
legal opinion of two eminent lawyers, the late Eugene Lafleur, K.C., and Mr. Aime Geoffrion, who both gave the opinion that while the senate had no right to originate a money bill, they had the right to amend it as fully as the House of Commons. On May 22, 1918, the senate adopted a report, which of course is an ex -parte document, setting forth certain conclusions. The first reads:
That the Senate of Canada has and always has had since it was created, the power to amend bills originating in the Commons appropriating any part of the revenue or imposing a tax by reducing the amounts therein, but has not the right to increase the same without the consent of the crown.
The House of Commons has never accepted the theory enunciated in the report from which I have just quoted, but has always contended that the senate has not the right to amend money bills, especially bills respecting taxation. As I have pointed out, it affects the balance of ways and means which the House of Commons has fixed to meet the expenditures for the following year, and this is certainly the prerogative and privilege of the House of Commons. As I say, the House of Commons has never conceded that claim of the senate; but in this instance the amendment is not, after all, so objectionable and has been accepted under protest.
Far from to-day's procedure creating a precedent, I find that there is even a formula in Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, form 59. The form there reads:
That the clerk do carry back the bill to the Senate and acquaint their honours that this house hath agreed to their amendments, the Minister of Finance accepting the said amendments with a protest against the right of the senate to make amendments to money bills.
Our motion to-day goes further than that, because it is more assertive of the rights of the commons. A conference would be useless. The senate is absolutely firm as to its rights, and we are equally firm on our side, but as I say, ultimately the question will have to be settled. I do not wish to say anything which might be misunderstood, but I believe it would be in the interests of the second chamber not to precipitate a conflict on this question.

speakeroldname: Hon. P. J. A. CARDIN (Minister of Public Works):
speechtext:
When the house rose last night we were considering harbours and rivers, proposed expenditures for the province of Quebec. The hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Stewart) had raised a question with regard to the proposed expenditure for Richelieu river improvement. This matter was discussed last year and the year before. It relates to the regulating of the flow of the Richelieu river by the erection of a dam which would retain the flow of water in the spring after dredging has been done, from St. Johns to the boundary. As far back as 1907 the United States authorities objected to this dredging being done. They contended that there existed in the bed of the river a natural obstruction to the flow of the water, and that if the obstruction were removed by dredging, the flow of the river would increase and thus lower the level of lake Champlain. At that time the proposal of a dam was discussed between the Canadian and the United States authorities, and the principle of a regulating dam was adopted by both countries. This dam is built with a certain number of sluices which can be opened in the spring when the water is high; as soon as the river comes to its natural level, the doors will be closed and the water will be kept at th; ' level in lake Champlain and the Richelieu river in the vicinity of the boundary.
The votes of last year, two years ago and this year have contemplated the carrying on 71492-305J
of that project, which is designed particularly to reclaim a large area of low land between St. Johns and the boundary. It is estimated that hundreds of thousands of dollars would be realized on these low lands if the water could be made to disappear more quickly in the spring. Under present conditions the water stays on these low lands so long that in most years it is impossible for the farmers to draw any benefit from their lands, owing as I have indicated, to the natural obstacles in the bed of the Richelieu river. If we disposed of those obstacles the water would flow away more rapidly, thus permitting cultivation of the low lands. But we cannot dredge that out without establishing a control of the flow of the river during the rest of the year.
These obstacles to which the minister refers would be below the dam?

No, above the dam. They prevent the water from flowing away quickly enough in the spring to allow cultivation of the low lands. But we cannot dispose of these natural obstacles, because if the channel were opened for the water to flow away more rapidly in the spring it would flow rapidly as well during the rest of the year, and the level of the water of lake Champlain would be lowered.
It seems to me that maintaining a dam to keep up the level of the water will defeat the object in view in removing the obstacles, unless the obstacles are below the dam.

Probably I am not making myself clear. At present there are obstacles in the river from St. Johns to the boundary. The river is not very deep. In the spring when the water is high in lake Champlain and in Canada adjoining the boundary the water cannot flow away rapidly enough on account of these natural obstacles. If we would dispose of these natural obstacles the problem would be solved; but we cannot dispose of them without providing a regulating system for the summer season. Therefore we are providing a dam in which the doors will be opened in the spring so that when the dredging is done the water will flow away as rapidly as possible. As soon as the high waters are disposed of the doors of the dam will be closed, keeping the water at the same level as it is at present, and thus avoiding any lowering of the level of lake Champlain.

I do not rise to oppose this vote, I simply want some information. I have made a thorough survey of the whole area and all around it on both sides of the river. The obstruction to which the minister
4850	COMMONS
Supply-Public Works-Harbours and Rivers
refers is just north of the city of St. Johns. It is a natural rock barrier in the river. The river flows over the rock in a sort of rapid, not a fall. Is the dam already constructed?
Yes.

The last time I was there it was not under construction. I have not had. time to go down this spring. I planned many times to go and make a survey but have not had time. The dam, I believe, is about six miles north of St. Johns-I have forgotten the name of the island.
Fryer's island.
When this vote first came up a few years ago I understood that it was to be part of a navigation scheme. Is it still part of a navigation scheme?

Yes, it is, because this dam is built practically half way, between St. Johns and Chambly. The present canal extends from St. Johns to Chambly. The length of it is twelve miles. The dam is being built six miles from Chambly. It reduces the length of the canalization by six miles.

That eliminates the small canal on the west side of the river. In other words the water level of lake Champlain will extend on down to the dam at Fryer's island. The low water level of lake Champlain, below which I do not see how the government can be permitted to lower it, is 93-3 feet above sea level. The high water level is 102-6 feet. The report given by the government, if I remember it correctly-I have not had time to familiarize myself with the facts-contained the statement that this dam would control the water level of lake Champlain and from lake Champlain to the dam, at 92-5 feet. I cannot find anywhere in the international agreement the consent of the United States to lowering the low water level from 93-3 to 92-5 feet. Have we that authority? It is not in the international report.
I am informed that the understanding that exists between the United States and Canada does not allow Canada to go below 92-5.
But you can go that low?
Yes, we can go that low.

Well, the dam has some merits; it will maintain the level of lake Champlain to six miles north of St. Johns.
I do not oppose, but I commented on the scheme in the beginning because I thought at that time it might be a waste of public money. It was to cost, I believe, in the 
neighbourhood of $12,000,000 to $15,000,000 when completed. We shall then have a waterway there of about twelve feet draft?
Yes.

Since the first locks, and the canal from Sorel south, are now of twelve feet draft, I do not feel that t'his money is going to be entirely wasted; there will be some benefit from it, though nothing at all comparable with the cost. That canal will be used but little anyway after it is completed; traffic is decreasing and never will increase in great magnitude. There are just a few oil boats going up and down there. Even on the United States end of the canal, from lake Champlain down to where the canal enters the Mohawk river, traffic is insignificant, notwithstanding the fact that there are substantial iron plants adjacent to lake Champlain. However, I no longer feel that the money will be totally wasted, and if the canal is to be completed I suppose year after year we shall have more votes until the work is finished from Fryer's island to Chambly basin.
The question of flooding has been emphasized, but if I were the minister I would not labour that point at all. The flooding does not amount to very much. I ascertained from Washington the height of lake Champlain as of the day I made my last survey, and they advised me that the water level was between 95 and 96 feet above sea level, or approximately four feet higher than the level at which this dam is to maintain lake Champlain. I did not find any flooding at 95 or 96 feet. The road immediately north of lake Champlain, which runs through a very pretty part of the country, was several feet above the water on that occasion. I discussed the question of flooding with the farmers and everyone else with whom I came in contact, and those to whom I spoke told me that at high water in the spring of the year, when I presume the water would be 102 feet above sea level, the road in front of the hotel might be a foot or two under water, but that condition did not prevail for very long. The land immediately north of the lake is largely swampy land, in any event, which could not be worked at all. There were only a few places where in the spring of the year the farmers were held off their land for perhaps a week or two. This bridge has been a matter of contention for some years now, starting in 1934 or 1935. The provincial government acquired permission to construct a new bridge, the major condition being, amongst other things to be done, that the centre span of the old railway bridge should be taken out. When the dominion government assume complete ownership of the old bridge they will have to consider seriously either financially helping the provincial government with the new bridge by a contribution, or taking out the centre span of the old bridge. Three railways are using the old bridge, and the revenue over a period of ten years has averaged $73,000 per annum. The expenditure has been high, running to an average of $48,000 per annum, but it has been high owing to the fact that up until a year or so ago the railway bridge was being used also for motor traffic; since the new bridge has been opened and the deck of the old bridge has been removed such expenditure will be no longer required. It is estimated that not over $20,000 to $25,000 will be necessary, which will mean that revenues of something like $50,000 per annum will accrue to the dominion government. The dominion government have been put to no expense for this old bridge. They would not have become owners but for the fact that the provincial government were told that they would not have permission to construct the new bridge, which is only two hundred feet from the present old bridge, unless these conditions were complied with. Having asked the provincial government to take out the centre span or hand over the bridge, the dominion government are now faced with having to take out the centre span themselves. They cannot take the attitude that the provincial government should do it, and then, when they become the owners, fail to do it themselves. It is very necessary that this centre span be taken out, because it is only 155 feet wide whereas the centre span of the new bridge is some 450 feet. Ships are passing through there almost every day; as a matter of fact last year the bridge was opened some 2,500 times. The new bridge has made it more hazardous for the ships, and in view of all the circumstances I make a plea to this government and the minister that since they have assumed responsibility for that bridge, the centre span will have to be removed. If not, the dominion government have no right to collect $50,000 a year without contributing to the cost of the new bridge.

I presume that on this item, Mr. Chairman, we may discuss matters of fundamental importance affecting the Department of Labour, with particular reference to the activities of the minister. With other hon. members I realize the vast amount of

hard work which the Minister of Labour has done since taking charge of the department, but we are now in the fourth and possibly the last session of this parliament, and after prorogation we may face dissolution. In the minds of a great many people, particularly those who have been looking to the Minister of Labour to do something to relieve unemployment, it may be disillusion rather than dissolution.
Hon. NORMAN McL. ROGERS (Minister of Labour): If my hon. friend will permit me, there is an item in the special supplementaries dealing with unemployment and grants in aid to the provinces, and I hope he will not mind my suggesting to him that that would be a more appropriate time to discuss unemployment than on the departmental estimates.

I have no objection to the course which the minister suggests, 'but I can assure him that if I make any comments now on the unemployment problem I shall not repeat them later. I have no desire to delay the proceedings, and intended to take only a few minutes to express my opinions with regard to the very serious unemployment situation. It was my purpose not to discuss the whole matter of unemployment on the departmental estimates, but rather to give a general summary of the unemployment situation.

My only thought was to have the discussion in proper sequence. If we have an unemployment debate on the main departmental estimates it might very well interrupt consideration of the specific items which are really before the committee.

Item agreed to.
101. Combines Investigation Act, $48,060.

I suggest that the
house consider the possibility of giving to the commissioner who handles this work a more direct method of action, or that we put into effect a form of action which will bring more direct results. We had presented under date of March 14, 1939, a report on the investigation of a combine in paperboard shipping containers, and if ever there was a combine

Supply-Labour-Combines Act
which was a combine this is one, according to the report of the commissioner. The report 6ays:
This system of control has been rigidly enforced. Deposits varying in amount from $500 to $10,000 were placed by the members with the management of the association as guarantees that prices would be maintained and that its other regulations would be observed. These deposits, in the ease of quota members, have been added to through a levy of one per cent on sales, until in 1938 the total accumulation amounted to over a quarter of a million dollars.
This is an accumulated fund, the financial backing for a combine. Further on the report says:
When these facts are considered, and when it is realized that the industry has operated until recently under a tariff protection which worked out to between forty and fifty per cent, it is apparent that price competition as a public safeguard in this industry has been all but completely suppressed by the operations of this association. Indeed it would be difficult to devise a more complete elimination of price competition in any industry than has been achieved through the operations of Container Materials, Limited, in connection with the manufacture and sale of shipping containers. Certainly nothing more complete in this respect has been the subject of investigation _ under the Combines Investigation Act since it was passed in 1923.
Then on page 86 I find this statement:
In the past five years four new corrugated box plants have been established in Ontario. The experience of one of these, O. and S. Corrugated Products Company, of Toronto, is related in section vi of this report.
Within a month of the establishment of the
O.	and S. Company the members of the combination induced its owners to agree to maintain the fixed prices, and secured this agreement by offering the company a sales allotment and a guarantee that even if the company produced nothing it would be compensated to the extent of $30,000 for its first nine months with the group. The sales of the O. and S. Company dropped sharply within a month of joining. Its sales for the entire nine months totalled only $19,355. Its receipts from the members of the combination for the same period amounted to $26,128.
In other words, this company was paid for its abstention from competition.
Arrangements on a similar basis continued, with the result that in the twenty-five months period ending April 30, 1938, payments received by this company from the group amounted to 84-5 per cent of its sales. In other words, under this arrangement, for every dollar of sales made by this company it received an addition of 84-5 cents from the other members of the combination. In this twenty-five months the O. and S. Company was paid a subsidy of $69,690, largely, if not altogether, as a return for its undertaking to refrain from any competition in price with the members of the combination. This amount was paid to this Ontario company in several instalments by all the members of Container Materials, Limited, including those whose plants are located in the maritime provinces, Manitoba and British Columbia.
Further with reference to this company, we have an illustration, from the evidence of how thoroughly it took advantage of the protection which had been given to it to exact the highest possible price which could be charged. In the evidence we find a statement from the Consumers' Glass Company, dated March 23, 1936, part of which reads as follows:
Despite the fact that we have approached the carton manufacturers in a friendly way in an endeavour to work out a cheaper carton to compete with American competition, it is now quite obvious to us that the carton companies are just toying -with our problems and intend to continue to take full advantage of the 50 per cent duty their industry enjoys. The exorbitant prices paid for cartons in Canada at this time is a very serious handicap to this industry and if satisfactory price arrangements cannot be arrived at between the two industries in a friendly way, we will have no other alternative but to take more drastic measures in the future.
One might go on and quote indefinitely from this document, but it all tends in the same direction. This was an admirable investigation; certainly the matter was thoroughly investigated. The report is, I think, a very able one and is a tribute to the able and conscientious administration of the Combines Investigation Act. But the difficulty lies in the fact that although this report is dated March 14, 1939, it seems impossible to do anything with .it so far, because of course in these matters we must go before the attorneys general of the different provinces. I am going to suggest later that there be a different method of approach.
A few days ago, on May 27, Mr. Shipman, a manufacturer of paper boxes who was outside the combine, wrote a letter to the commissioner of customs and sent me a copy. I desire to quote from his letter:
On October 1, 1938, the price of liner board, for instance, was $1.56 per thousand square feet, to-day it is $1.30 per M square feet, a reduction of 16| per cent. During this same period, the combine members who, as you know', also manufacture and control the price of paper board have reduced their prices of boxes as follows: October 1, 1938, 20 per cent; January, 1939, 3 per cent; February, 1939, 5 per cent; March, 1939, 10 per cent; making a total of 38 per cent. In addition to cutting the price of boxes 38 per cent the O. & 8. Corrugated Products Company openly offer all our customers to beat the above prices by 5 per cent and in some cases more than that, bearing the cost of same, we believe, from monies received from the combine members.
I do not know whether this gentleman is right or not, but it is a suggestion that the combine continues to exist, but that, in changed circumstances, desiring now to get rid of the only competitor that remains-one of the original disturbers of their combine- they propose to put him out of business, right
Supply-Labour-Combines Act

under the shadow of their combine, by means of continuing reductions in prices far below a level which might normally be expected.
Surely under these circumstances, where a combine still continues in sharp defiance of the report of the commissioner, or the report is deliberately ignored, it might be well for the House of Commons to consider another remedy and, I suggest, a potent one. It lies in section 15 of the Customs Tariff, which provides:
1.	Whenever the governor in council deems it to be in the public interest to inquire into any conspiracy, combination, agreement or arrangement alleged to exist among manufacturers or dealers in any article of commerce to unduly promote the advantage of the manufacturers or dealers in such article at the expense of the consumers, the governor in council may commission or empower any judge of the supreme court, or of the Exchequer Court of Canada, or of any superior court or county court in Canada, to hold an inquiry in a summary way and report to the governor in council whether such conspiracy, combination, agreement or arrangement exists.
In regard to this section of the Customs Tariff I should like to ask the minister if now, with a report such as this, we have not the definite suggestion that a combine does exist. We then come to the remedy:
2.. The judge may compel the attendance of witnesses and examine them under oath and require the production of books and papers, and shall have such other necessary powers as are conferred upon him by the governor in council for the purpose of such inquiry.
The information referred to has been already submitted.
3. If the judge reports that such conspiracy, combination, agreement or arrangement exists in respect of such article, the governor in council may admit the article free of duty, or so reduce the duty thereon as to give to the public the benefit of reasonable competition in the article, if it appears to the governor in council that such disadvantage to the consumer is facilitated by the duties of customs imposed on a like article.
I submit that the case is now proven, that a remedy exists within the Customs Tariff, and that, in order to make effective the work of the combines investigation officer, where a case has been proven against the combine, action may be taken under the clause of the Customs Act which I have cited. It is a far more powerful and forceful remedy than any other that can be had under the Combines Investigation Act. Before the Combines Investigation Act can be made really effective there must be some coordination between the administration of the Customs Tariff and the operation of the combines act so that when it is shown that this state of affairs exists and that these companies, coldbloodedly and remorselessly, have been

exploiting the people months after the investigation has taken place, the government can step in. The hand which can stop them, which has power to take away the monopoly which the same hand gave, should be reached out so strongly and forcefully that the first time action is taken it will be a lesson to other corporations that there are limits to human greed. Let it be a lesson to all such corporations that within the Customs Tariff we have the power to impose a further restraint upon their activities.

The Combines Investigation Act itself provides three types of remedy. There is first of all the remedy of publicity, which in certain cases in the past has been effective, and has brought about a correction of the situation complained of within a given industry. In addition to that there are penalties, consisting of fines of $10,000 and $25,000 against individuals and corporations respectively, with a further provision for imprisonment. Finally the act provides for the alternative remedy to which the hon. member has referred, namely, the removal or reduction of the customs duty which apparently has permitted the combine to carry on its illegal operations. This provision is found not only in the Customs Tariff but in the combines act itself. It is actually incorporated in that statute. In the particular investigation under discussion, into the manufacture and sale of paperboard shipping containers and related products-
The second remedy to which the minister refers can be applied only after further action in the courts-
Correct.
*-by the attorney general, and after conviction has been obtained.

Yes. I was going to explain that the report in this case was made by the commissioner on March 14 of this year. On March 31, after printing, it was transmitted to the attorneys general of the six provinces in which the combine was found to be carrying on its operations. This practice is laid down definitely in the terms of the Combines Investigation Act and it has been followed from the beginning, from the time the original legislation was adopted in 1923; and only once where the report and evidence have been transmitted to the attorney general of a province has prosecution failed to follow. The other remedy to which the hon. member refers is available to be exercised at discretion by the governor in council, but I submit that in order to carry out the purpose of the act it is certainly desirable in the first instance

Supply-Labour-Combines Act
to follow the normal procedure of transmitting the report and the evidence to the attorney general who has charge of the administration of justice in the province in which the combine has been found to exist.
During the past year another report was made, in connection with the distribution of tobacco products in Alberta and elsewhere in Canada. The same procedure was followed there, namely, the transmission of the report and the evidence to the attorney general of the province of Alberta. In pursuance of that, the attorney general of Alberta has commenced proceedings against this alleged tobacco combine and those proceedings are now in progress. Any other action such as that suggested by my hon. friend would certainly be collateral to the normal procedure and it would be for the governor in council in each case to determine whether upon the merits it was desirable to apply this further remedy, the reduction or removal of the tariff on the commodity in question.

Arising out of the minister's remarks are one or two questions which I should like him to answer. In the first place, does he regard publicity as an adequate punishment for a business record such as is revealed in the combine recently investigated, the paperboard shipping container matter? Secondly, how many times has the fine of $10,000 been imposed in Canada within recent years? And while the Combines Investigation Act contains a clause in regard to the reduction of duties, has that provision ever -been enforced? If so, who has enforced it? Have we ever had an application of the section of the Customs Tariff under which the duty was reduced in order to check the operations of a combine? I would suggest that the offence which these men have committed is not merely that of charging a higher price, because the tariff gives them permission, but it is the fact that they have brought about a combine which is effective in preventing competition and preventing others from lowering the price. Finally I submit that their offence, because it affects the national life of Canada, is a national matter and that action should properly be taken by the federal government. It is a crime against the consumers and the industry of the nation and therefore differs from other offences on which court action might be taken.
As to the fines which have been imposed and collected under the act since its inception, the total from 1923 to 1939 amounted to $316,400.
How much within the last five years?

From 1932 the fines have been:
Electric Estimators Association of Toronto,

Canadian Fruit Basket Pool, $1,500.
Anthracite coal importers, $43,500.	[DOT]
What were the dates of the last three?
The Canadian Basket Pool was January, 1933, and the anthracite coal December, 1933, and January, 1935.
Is that the last?
Yes.

It is a pleasure for one to be in agreement with a part of the remarks of the hon. member for Huron North, and I rise to commend some of the things he has said. I will not take time to point out those statements that I commend. With reference to one industry which he mentioned, it is common knowledge in the trade that the box industry-fibre boxes, corrugated boxes and so on-has such a grip on the box requirements of Canada that those engaged in that industry are simply hurting themselves in the long run and opening up possibilities of imports of vast quantities of fibreboard and corrugated boxes and packages which will come largely from the southern states. Ultimately this will be a great detriment to Canada. So that any effort put forth by the department with a view to the carrying out of the provisions of this act will be for the benefit of Canada. Let me give one or two instances of what is actually happening. Suppose a manufacturer who is using a certain corrugated box, say 18 by 12 by 9 inches, thinks he can make a saving by reducing that 9 inches to 8J inches. If he sends out a request to half a dozen different sources for a quotation on fifty thousand cartons, he gets exactly the same price from all the organizations manufacturing that particular carton. If his business is in Windsor, and he asks for quotations from Windsor, London, Guelph, Kitchener and Toronto, with Kitchener as the point of delivery, all these branches of the industry-and they are all different firms- will quote the same delivered price. If the buyers are in Kitchener and have a trucking service running between Kitchener and Toronto and wish to buy the cartons in Toronto in order to get a return load for their trucks and absorb the trucking charges themselves, they still get no consideration. In other words the manufacturer of the cartons in Toronto will deliver or pay the freight into Kitchener but will make no deduction if
Supply-Labour-Combines Act

delivery is taken in Toronto. There is, in short, a tight combine with regard to that particular product.
What obtains in that industry obtains also in other industries. As I said in another connection .some little while ago-the minister rather ridiculed the idea-let us have a little strength and activity in the administration of this act. When I said to him a year or two ago that it was time we had some strong men determined on action in matters of this kind, I meant every word I said, and I reiterate it now. Instead of fussing around about provincial jurisdiction and that sort of thing with regard to prosecuting these cases, let him take action quickly, not only on behalf of those who find it necessary to purchase large supplies of this kind, but on behalf of Canada generally. As a result of this particular combine the purchasing is being done in a country where the workmanship on the product does not inure to the benefit of Canada. Any action taken by the minister along the line of the comments of the hon. member for Huron North will 'be welcome to the people of Canada.

I take it that the Combines Investigation Act is in good working order. What procedure must be followed in order to get the machinery in operation? Is it necessary that a request be made of the government or does the government undertake to proceed on its own initiative? I am thinking now of the combine which most of us agree exists in the manufacture of farm machinery. We had a federal investigation, and while we did not report that a combine actually exists, we did suggest that there was no competition in prices. For all practical purposes a combine really exists in regard to farm machinery. The Saskatchewan government carried on a similar investigation and they declared emphatically that a combine did exist. We all know that an investigation was held in the United States and it was definitely found that an international combine existed, and one of the companies named as being in that combine was our own Massey-Harris Company of Canada. In effect that obligation is to bring to the attention of the competent

legislative authority such conventions as have been adopted by the international labour organization. Up to 1935 the practice followed was for the Minister of Labour to table these conventions as they were received, and they were made available in so far as they were within the competence of this parliament. With respect to matters which fell within provincial jurisdiction, the practice was to transmit the conventions without delay to the lieutenant governors of the various provinces. In 1935 the previous administration took the position that by ratification of an international labour convention the dominion parliament could of itself acquire complete authority to enact the legislation necessary to carry the convention into effect. That was the whole basis of the legislation passed by this parliament which dealt with hours and with wages-the minimum wage bill, the weekly day of rest, and the eight hour day. A question arose as to the validity of that legislation, and, in particular, as to the sufficiency of the contention that the dominion parliament, merely by ratifying the convention, could acquire a jurisdiction which by the constitution was definitely assigned to the provincial legislatures. The matter -was taken to the privy council. The privy council rejected the contention that ratification of the international labour convention gave legislative authority to this parliament to carry the convention into effect. That being the case, it was necessary for this government to revert to the former practice in carrying out its obligations as a member of the international labour organization. In other words, we must table here the conventions which are competent for this parliament, and transmit to the provinces the conventions the subject matter of which falls within provincial jurisdiction.

This worker has been working out away from home for two years, she comes from a large family-ten children- who are poor and she needs the money for clothes, times are so hard that she cannot stay at home, she has worked for my mother all this last winter and I want to get the payments for her if possible for this last winter's work which she has done. My mother's sickness is partly a nervous disorder with high blood pressure and she has to have someone looking after her whom she knows, that is why she has to have someone from this neighbourhood. In my own family my father died about eighteen months ago and before that two of my brothers died, making unavoidable expenses. In this worker's family there has been also a terrible amount of sickness for the last ten months. She is eighteen years of age and she needs this money very badly and I am unable to pay it myself. I could give you the names of many neighbours who would tell you that these facts are correct. I might say that last winter 1937-38 her sister worked for my mother under similar conditions and the government gave her the payments without any trouble.
He goes on to tell of several similar cases. Cases of this sort ought in some way be allowed to come in under the plan. I understand the provincial authorities say they can do nothing with such cases because of the federal regulations. I have here the file of correspondence that passed between the department at Regina and the leader of the opposition in the Saskatchewan legislature. I notice that in the last letter the reason is given as follows:
I am directed by the Hon. R. J. M. Parker to acknowledge your letter to him under date of April 26 regarding the above application.
We notified (the lady) on December 20 the reason for the rejection of 'her application, namely, that a worker must have been maintaining herself independent of her home during the period of at least one year immediately preceding the application. We notified her again on January 19 that we could not change our decision contained in our previous communication. We explained the reason for the rejection again on February 24 and then again on March 30.
For your information I am sending you a copy of her application made on November 29, from which you will notice that the only work that she did during the past twelve months was during May and June. For this reason the auditors will not pass it, and I am unable to accept same.
I am drawing this matter to the attention of the minister as typical in the hope that there may be an adjustment. As I said at the outset, I have found the department ready to give sympathetic consideration at all times. This letter came to my hand this afternoon, and I thought I would place it before the

minister for his consideration now and in the future, because it states the case better than I could.

My hon. friend, I am sure, understands that some 30,000 cases were dealt with in Saskatchewan, and that in the nature of things there would be some rejections which might be open to question. We have dealt with a large number of individual complaints with respect to rejections, and some corrections have been made; in other cases the rejections have been upheld. But I can assure the hon. member that every case will be dealt with on its merits.

I said at the outset that I appreciate the courtesy and consideration of the minister. I am bringing this to his attention, as a typical case, not because I am criticizing his department. I believe if the minister had reviewed this case himself the decision might have been different. I shall pass it on to him at the close of the sitting.

I presume this is the item on which the minister suggested we might discuss the general question of unemployment. It is not my intention to deal with it at any length. We are now in the fourth session of this parliament. Probably in the course of a few days parliament will prorogue; prorogation may be followed by dissolution, and it is quite possible that we may not be able to see the minister until at least after another election, assuming everything goes as the minister expects.
You may not see him then.

I am not going to discuss the election, but for a few moments I wish to deal with the occasion when the minister first came to this house, almost four years ago. As I said at three o'clock this afternoon, the minister has been one of the most hardworking ministers in the government. I think every hon. member recognizes the great amount of hard, conscientious work that he has done. Of all the ministers perhaps the Minister of Labour has the most thankless task at the present time. I should be inclined to put as the next most difficult department that of the Minister of Finance, who is trying to make two plus two equal six. But I believe the Department of Labour has an even more difficult task than the Department of Finance, because it is trying to remedy a condition within certain prescribed limits which I think make success almost impossible.
I remember the time when the minister made his first speech in this house, which to me was somewhat of a disappointment, in
view of the splendid reputation he had when he first came here as Minister of Labour. I am not going to say that his reputation has been dimmed in the meantime, but with the high hopes we had of him then as a man of fine sympathies and ideals, one might have expected that he would find some effective means of dealing with the very difficult problem of unemployment which to-day faces us in almost exactly the same proportions as at the time the minister took office. Looking back to the last election, to the hopes held out by the Liberal party, to their promises as to what they would do if returned to power, one can readily realize how disappointed a great many people must be to-day when they find the unemployment problem just as serious as it was in 1935.
When the minister first spoke in this house on unemployment a few years ago-the minister will correct me if I am wrong, I am speaking entirely from memory-he said the government were taking a long-range view of the whole situation. This long-range view has now had a few years in which to operate, and so far the results of its operation have not been very successful. He laid down certain specific rules so far as he himself was concerned and certain ideas on which he would work. All those ideas have: been of little avail in controlling unemployment in Canada.
I think the minister said at the time that private employers had some responsibility in this matter. To-day most of us recognize that private capital has made very little contribution towards the solution of this problem. And where private capital has so completely failed in its responsibility, that of the government is all the greater; yet the policies of the government during the past few years have been more or less a failure. The minister may tell the committee that the government have adopted certain measures, have done certain things along certain lines. I am looking at this problem however, not in a piecemeal way but as a whole. So far as the general situation in Canada is concerned, there has really been no general policy adopted by the government to end unemployment, and the unemployed have very little to look forward to in the immediate future in the way of remedial action.
The policies of the government over the past few years have been a failure. The idea of finding markets abroad for our surplus products has proven of no avail in the unusual times in which we are living. I believe the minister realizes that you cannot remedy the conditions which have developed in the last few years by old fashioned methods. If we are to deal effectively with the problems

which confront us to-day, we shall have to use some modem technique. Other countries are attempting to do something, yet we have done nothing very different from what the former government did from 1930 to 1935.

Will my hon. friend permit one question? He has said that other countries have attempted certain policies. He acknowledged a while ago that this government has followed certain policies. Has he found any country which, having attempted by various measures to cure unemployment, has succeeded in a way which satisfies him?

It is difficult for one who lives in Canada to speak of nations far away, where he cannot give definite examples from his personal observation. But in New Zealand, where I know they have difficulties to contend with greater than ours, they have made a definite effort to deal with the problem of unemployment, and I was informed no later than this afternoon that there is practically no unemployment in New Zealand.
But there are grave doubts whether that position can be maintained.

Yes, I admit that. I say their difficulties are greater than ours because they have not the same rich natural resources in that small country that we have in Canada. The physical condition of the country is such that they are compelled to depend very largely in many respects upon imports for the basis of their existence. On the other hand in Canada we have to face difficulties which in New Zealand they probably have not to contend with. Our difficulties may be of a constitutional nature, but I suggest that it should be much easier to overcome constitutional difficulties than to overcome the physical handicaps that exist in other countries, and I feel sure that if we devoted only half the effort that has been expended in New Zealand, for example, to overcoming these difficulties, we should be in a much better position than we are to-day.
Some of the continental countries, such as Sweden and others, have made at least some effort to deal with the problem. My hon. friends may say, "Well, see what has happened in the United States, where they have spent vast sums in trying to deal with the problem, and yet they find themselves in a position similar to that of a few years ago." Well, I would far rather see our government make an effort to deal with the problem and fail than to make no effort at all. We have made no real effort. Since the government came to power in 1935 they have merely gone along the same old road; relief-doles if you

want to call it that-and public works. That is no solution, nor can it ever be a solution of our unemployment problem.
What does my hon. friend suggest in addition, other than to stimulate trade, which he forgot to mention?
That has been a failure too.

What does my hon. friend
suggest?
I would suggest that you go along new lines.
What new lines?
I would suggest that we so control the natural resources of this country as to give the people a much higher standard of living than they enjoy at the present time.
That is not an answer.

My hon. friend wants definite legislation? Then I would say first there is the control of finance, and in addition, in the platform of our own party there are many suggestions for dealing with this situation.
Such as what?
The government could have undertaken a housing scheme.
We are doing that.

But it is picayune as compared to what the government could have done; it is very small. They could have undertaken a series of public works much greater than has been undertaken up to the present time.
My hon. friend says that is no solution.
It is no solution, but it is a palliative.
But my hon. friend wants something more than a palliative.

It would be a palliative until such time as the government could bring about remedial conditions which would give the people of this country a greater share "of the wealth produced in Canada. I might in this regard even refer the minister to some of the promises made by the Liberal party, through the Prime Minister, during the last campaign. There is no use in saying we cannot do these things; there is no reason for saying there may be constitutional difficulties in the way. I believe that with the control of finance, which is under federal jurisdiction; with control of the tariffs and with the vast amount of money that is being spent by this government, we could have done something far more effective than anything that has been

Supply-Labour-Federal Contributions
done up to the present. As far as I can gather from the minister, the government have nothing further to suggest to the country beyond what they have done or attempted to do in the last few years, namely relief, public works and an attempt to expand the trade of the country.
What else is there?
I did not come prepared to offer any definite suggestions; I did not even intend to go into that aspect of the question.

I want to be fair to my hon. friend but I want him to be fair to me also. He is accusing us of not having followed sound methods in dealing with unemployment, but he has not been able to suggest any alternatives to the methods that have been followed, namely, stimulating private employment through trade policies, stimulating public employment through public works, and providing through relief measures for those who are unemployed and unable to take care of themselves.

The government might have attempted a good many things. They could have reduced the age limit in connection with old age pensions, which would have removed a good many people from industry and given an opportunity to younger people.
That would be just transferring them, putting more on relief.
Oh, no.
Oh, yes.

That is a matter of opinion. We believe in reducing the hours of labour, though I suppose we shall be met with the reply that this is entirely a matter of provincial jurisdiction. We would reduce the hours of labour; we would try to maintain a greater volume of purchasing power among the great masses of the people, which would mean that they could consume far more of the wealth of the country than is now being *consumed.' Within the last few weeks the government have done that, not from choice but from necessity. I refer to the item appearing in the estimates which provides 81,000,000 for the free distribution of butter. That million dollars' worth of butter is being distributed to-day to those who need it. If we establish that principle as far as butter is concerned, why can we not do it in regard to other commodities? I do not say we should give away these goods. I am opposed to the dole system; I want to see every person capable of working perform some useful function in society. So I say to the government and to the minister that if the policy they
have followed during the last few years has failed, it is time they looked around and found some other means of coping with this very difficult and important problem, which has been with us not only since this government came into power but since 1930. When we are told that this is a temporary problem, I do not agree; any situation that has existed for nine years can almost be called a permanent aspect of the economic life of the country. The question, as we have always suggested, is whether any government can, within the confines of the capitalistic structure, eradicate unemployment from our midst. Personally I am doubtful. I do not know the minister's point of view; he may hold other opinions, but if the old remedies have failed it is the duty of the government and of parliament to find new remedies to deal with the problem, but as far as I know the government have nothing to offer.
Within the next few days members of this house will be returning to their constituencies and will be meeting their constituents; and, as I said a moment or so ago, we may be faced with an election. No doubt we shall have to meet thousands of people. I represent a fairly large industrial constituency; and looking back over the four years this government have been in power, with one of the largest majorities ever given to a party in the history of this dominion, I am just wondering what I can tell my constituents as to anything definite the government have accomplished in dealing with one of the most pressing problems of the day. What can I say to them? When the government came to office in 1935 there were approximately 460,000 people out of work. Now, in 1939, we have fully as many people, and probably more, out of work. The situation is not improving by any means. The government came into power in 1935 on an upswing in the industrial life of this country, which reached its highest point in 1937 or thereabouts. Since 1937 employment has tended to decrease; in other words the cycle is against the government at the present time so what can we tell the unemployed? After all, I do not agree with some of the statements which have been made concerning the unemployed, but which I shall not repeat this afternoon. What can I tell the unemployed in my constituency, of whom there are thousands? Can I tell them we have tried the dole and that we have tried relief, but that we have not accomplished anything?
There is nothing more demoralizing to any community than to keep large numbers on a perpetual dole, as has happened in my con-

stituency. I wish it could be avoided, and that we might find some effective means of providing employment. Demoralization is creeping into the minds of our young people, and of our older generation, and it is that to which I am so much opposed, and which I should like to see eradicated from our midst. I want to see all our people becoming useful and productive citizens, but if we continue to keep them on the dole, in time they will become practically unemployable.
We have tried the dole; we have tried relief and we have tried public works-all to no avail. We have tried to extend our markets. We can find no markets for our goods, and for reasons which must be obvious to any hon. member. If we cannot find markets, are we going to continue in our present fashion, with enormous wealth in the form of wheat, foodstuffs, clothing and other materials which our people cannot utilize because something stands in their way? Why can we not find ways and means whereby the great masses of our people would gain access to the means of life which should be the birthright of every Canadian?
I am prompted to make these extemporaneous observations this afternoon because I believe, in common with other hon. members, that this parliament as at present constituted may not meet again. If I have to face the electors in the near future, all I can say is that I am more than disappointed, not so much with the Minister of Labour, because he is merely a reflection of the attitude of the government, but because the government have not taken more drastic steps to deal with one of the most important problems with which the country is faced.

Mr. Chairman, for some time past certain members of the opposition, both Conservative and Social Credit, have been making the city of Hull the butt of their criticism, among others the hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Landeryou) who on May 12th, when the house was discussing the contribution of 810,000 to the international commission for the assistance of Spanish child refugees, asked the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Michaud) whether the total amount of this grant was used up, I shall quote what he said on that occasion:
It is too bad, because there are all kinds of Canadian child refugees in the city of Hull who are in need of relief. Will the minister consider using any portion that has not been used, for Canadian refugee children in the city of Hull?
I interjected:
May I interrupt the hon. member? There is nobody suffering in Hull.
tMr. Heaps.]
The reporter did not complete my sentence; he did not reproduce my words accurately. What I said was this: "There is nobody suffering in Hull because of the grant of $10,000 for the Spanish child refugees." Yesterday during the discussion of the estimates of the Department of Fisheries the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Pelletier) repeated the words of the hon. member for Calgary East:
It is too bad, because there are all kinds of Canadian child refugees in the city of Hull who are in need of relief. Will the minister consider using any portion that has not been used, for Canadian refugee children in the city of Hull?
I cannot contradict the statements of these hon. members as regards the presence of refugees in the city of Hull, but I have to admit at once that I am unaware of there being any refugees there. The inquiries I have made show that the increase of population in Hull in recent years has been normal. Not only did I make inquiries in that connection, but I also looked up, for the benefit of the hon. member for Peace River the definition of the word refugee. The Larousse dictionary defines it as follows:
A person who has fled his country to avoid persecution or condemnation.
I am unaware of the presence in my city of children who have left their native country because they were persecuted or convicted of an offence. An English dictionary defines "refugees" as follows:
Persons escaped to foreign countries from religious or political persecution.
I have quoted the words of these two hon. gentlemen literally because I have found that every word I ever uttered in this house-and I have not uttered many, thank God!-have been misinterpreted. I therefore assert unhesitatingly that there are no refugees in the city of Hull.
As to unemployment, it exists not only here but also in Alberta. Although the members of the Social Credit Group spend part of their time in my home city and other parts of my constituency boasting of what is being done in Alberta. The discussions which take place in this house indicate there is unemployment in Alberta as everywhere else.
This morning, while discussing the estimates of the Department of Public Works, the same hon. member for Peace River complained to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cardin) that the province of Alberta was not receiving its due share of grants. One good reason for that, if it is true, is that Alberta's representatives seem more inclined to interfere with the affairs of others than to attend to their own. I would like to point out to the hon. member for Calgary East, that he knows nothing what-

ever of conditions in the city of Hull. He may have received reports from discontented persons especially from the unemployed who cannot obtain everything they wish. The hon. member for Peace River, who should keep the peace himself at times, is equally uninformed about conditions in my city. If the hon. members were to come there and make a thorough study of the matter; if they were to take into account the recent history of the city, they would realize that Hull is in a position which, if not flourishing, can at least be favourably compared with that of other cities, and even of those where the hon. members reside. While these gentlemen deliver lectures on social credit in Hull, and end their meetings by passing the hat around, thus extracting from the unemployed a portion of the money they need to live, while they distribute in the meeting-hall, for cash, certain publications entitled "Instructor and Protector," the member for Hull is going about his parliamentary duties, though perhaps not always in the House. I can assure the hon. member for Peace River that I have rendered greater services to the less fortunate voters in my city than he ever will through sermons such as he delivered lately in Buckingham and other parishes in my riding.
The member for Peace River is a young man; I have heard him discuss in this house constitutional and legal matters, and, to my mind, the subject matter of these discussions appeared to be far beyond his power to grasp. I believe that if he were to listen more often to other speakers in the house rather than participate in debates whereof he knows nothing, he would eventually be in a position to render great services, not only to his riding or to his province, but to the country as a whole. I have this much to say to him: I have never attacked, nor spoken against social credit members or their activities within their province. That is their own business. But when they invade our province, I would ask them, at least, not to deceive those who are of good faith, and especially the class of people who are most in need of relief. When they travel through different parishes in our province, proclaiming, that as soon as they come into power they will organize a free distribution of wealth, and that poverty will disappear from the land, I do not think they are carrying on a work that can be useful to the province, or to the country at large. At all events, I wish to advise them that, during the many battles I have had to wage in the past, although I am not very old, I have always noticed that those who stuck to the truth whenever they opposed a Liberal candidate in the Hull riding, were the ones who had the greatest success, and that those who
resorted to low methods, inevitably lost their deposit, and there are many in the past who did lose their deposit. I challenge anyone of the Social Credit representatives who have delivered speeches in my riding-and I know everyone of them-to stand there at the forthcoming general election, and I guarantee that he shall have the same fate as the rest.
Let us now examine what has been accomplished in Hull as regards unemployment. During the last fifteen years, three large industries have left that city: first, the Eddy match factory which was sold to the World Match Company, and which formerly employed about 600 persons. This industry moved to Berthier and Pembroke, but the former employees of the Eddy Match Company did not leave the city as the result of its sale to the World Match Company.
Another company, owned by P. H. Dupuis, which traded in building materials and employed at least 300 workmen, not perhaps during the whole year, but throughout the summer. The owner died and his employees were unable to find work elsewhere.
I could easily speak at length on conditions in Hull, conditions with which you are not at all familiar, if I thought that, after giving you a great deal of information which you do not possess on the subject, you might be less inclined to meddle in the affairs of that city. The Gilmour mill, which employed about 300 persons throughout the summer, was sold to the International Paper Company.
During the last fifteen years, these plants which employed 1,200 persons have disappeared from Hull and there have been no others to take their place. Our people are so attached to the city and county of Hull that they have been unwilling to move to other parts of the country-a thing on the other hand, which I would not advise them to do. Having lost their jobs, these people remained in our city, endeavouring to find manual labour elsewhere. And that is the reason for the present unemployment situation in Hull.
From 1931 to 1935, direct relief was granted, toward the cost of which, I believe, the federal and provincial governments and the city of Hull each contributed one third. In 1936, a short while after their coming into power, the Duplessis government abolished the direct relief system and replaced it by unemployment works projects. The provincial authorities have spent large amounts in our city and they now claim, it would seem, that it is due to the expenditure of provincial funds alone that between 1,200 and 1,500 persons received employment for a certain period of time. The moment they realized these unemployment projects were proving very costly, the pro-

The federal government has spent in my constituency in the last couple of years more money than in many other counties I know of. A protection wall has been constructed along the Ottawa river. Though not completed it has cost the Department of Public works close to $67,000. Only the genuine unemployed were given work on this job *-not the kind of unemployed men who spend their time on the street with the pamphlets which you sell to them for 25 cents each seeking to indoctrinate other young people against our present democratic system, but the real unemployed-and their names can be obtained from the Department of Public Works.
There has also been erected in my town a drill hall which has cost, including land and improvements, about S200.000. The works I have mentioned have been executed during the past two years.
Recently, this spring, when there was distress to relieve, the Department of Labour transferred to the Federal District Commission a sum of $35,000 to spend in the section of the county of Wright adjoining the city of Hull and also in my county, on Kettle island. The names of the men employed at this work were supplied to me by the municipal councils of the neighbouring parishes, one of which is Gatineau Mills, where you held a euchre party at which you spoke before only 26 persons. In that place the government gave work to 46 persons during six weeks.

During the past year the federal government granted $400,000 a month to the province of Quebec. The provincial government was free to spend this money where they pleased. Whether they spent it in Hull or elsewhere, the dominion government is not to be blamed. Neverthless, I think more could be done in my county. I shall not ask the hon. member who will probably speak after me to support the requests I present to the federal government every day. The ministers whom I visit most often are those whose departments have the most money to spend. I try to have the money distributed in such a manner as to provide employment where it is most needed, and if I am reproached with speaking infrequently in the house, I can answer you that while the hon. member was speaking I was attending to the interests of my constituents. And should other statements of that kind be made and my words not be accurately quoted, I shall have to make another speech in order to set matters right.
You will admit, Mr. Chairman, that we finally have succeeded in getting the member for Hull to say something, which was previously impossible.
You made him lose his time.

I want to remind the hon. member that we have said nothing against him personally. We had no intention of criticizing but we wanted to find a solution to our economic problems. I know that the hon. member for Hull is daily engaged in trying to get public works, unemployment relief and so on, but I must say that all his efforts are within the present economic system which, according to our theory, cannot provide a permanent solution to the unemployment problem. We acknowledge that the government and the hon. members are doing their best, we even admit they are persevering in their endeavour. It was my privilege to congratulate the hon. minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) and to tell him that he is the best qualified man in the Liberal party to perform the heavy duties of the administration of the Department of Labour. I told him that notwithstanding all his remarkable qualifications and all his university degrees, notwithstanding the help of the hon. the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) and the advice of the right hon. the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), he has been unable to find a permanent solution to the unemployment problem, the effects of which are felt all over the country.

I disagree with the hon. member for Hull when he says that I am not concerned with the distress which exists in Hull. I am a federal member, and it is not only my right but also my duty to look after the economic conditions of the people. If the situation that exists in Hull is brought up it is because some poor people of that city, forced by dire necessity to do things which they would never have done otherwise, have supplied us with the necessary information so that we might bring their case before the authorities.
The situation of the refugees has been mentioned. I do not think it is necessary to read the affidavits showing that children have to be taken care of by friends because their own father is out of work. I know just as well as the government and as the hon. members that distressing conditions exist in Hull. The object we are aiming at is to bring a change in our economic system so as to solve permanently the present conditions, instead of going on spending money for public works or unemployment relief.
Are you opposed to public works?

I only say that public works are but a temporary remedy and do not solve the economic problem. That is why I invite the members of the Liberal party

who are always very nice to me, I admit-to come to our meetings so as to study the question and to help us find a permanent solution to the unemployment problem.
You will not attain your object through demagogy.

Of course, Mr. Speaker, a solution of the unemployment problem has not yet been found by the government. I notice that the Minister of Labour insisted that the hon. member for Winnipeg North who was speaking a few moments ago, should give his solution. Thereby the minister candidly admitted that he could not find any solution. Of course we have often urged in this house that the solution did not lie along the present lines, and that fact is amply proved by the results which have been achieved. What we should like to see done is a study made of the causes of unemployment. From time to time the minister has said that such a thing cannot be done, that it covers too wide a field, that we can never ascertain the causes of unemployment. My answer is that until we go to work and set up the necessary authority to find out what is causing unemployment and why our economic system is not functioning in the way it should do, we shall not reach any solution. I realize as well as he 71492-3074
does that there are external causes, but that is not an answer to the demand that of our own accord we should set up a body to study the conditions which affect the internal economy of this country. From time to time we have suggested ways and means of bringing about a satisfactory solution, but the theories we have advanced have been ridiculed and more or less condemned without proper examination. It is not in that fashion that our economic problems of to-day will be solved. We contend that in the course of our contributions to the debates in this house we have suggested various measures which the government could have examined with profit and attempted to adopt in order to bring about an amelioration of the conditions which we face in these times. I say advisedly " attempted to," because the minister will not concede that there is any one solution of the problem, but contends that it must be found in many parts of our economic system. I am inclined to agree with him. but I repeat that until he goes to work to try to ascertain the cause of unemployment the problem will never be solved.

With unanimous consent. Mr. ROGERS: The statement is as follows: Dominion Unemployment Relief
Ottawa, April 21, 1939.
Trans-Canada Highway The trans-Canada highway is designated, in dominion-provincial agreements, under relief legislation, as follows:
"such provincial highway or highways affording a continuous route connecting the province *with any other or others of the provinces as has been designated by the province and approved by the dominion."
The trans-Canada highway, when completed from Halifax to Vancouver, will be approximately 4,317 miles, including 52 miles of highway in the province of Prince Edward Island.

It has been part of my responsibility this session as a member of the opposition to take particular interest in his department; and I am very happy indeed at this stage, in the dying hours of the session, to pay tribute to the minister's good nature, his patience and his sportsmanship. I only wish that I could speak in equal terms of his administration, which has been to many a bitter disappointment.
