I regret to have to rise on this question of external affairs, but I have a matter to bring to the attention of the government. In Estcourt, in the state of Maine, just south of Temiscouata county, there is a
Supply-External Affairs

man named Ouellette, a barber, who has a beer licence. There are only six United States families in the neighbourhood, but of course he secured that licence in order to sell beer to Canadians who cross the border to go to his barber shop to drink beer. I have had strong protests from reliable sources in that district saying it is very bad for youth to go there to drink beer in this place.
Of, course there have been a great many abuses in that district, on the part of the United States authorities as much as on the part of some of the United States residents. I wonder what is the use of maintaining a Department of External Affairs, with legations throughout the world, when that department and the Canadian legation at Washington do not care to look into these matters and try to arrange adjustments satisfactory to the people concerned. The farmers there have been the victims of abuse on the part of United States customs officials, and now one of these Americans, who probably pulls the strings for an increase in tariff, has been successful in obtaining this licence. I want the minister, who knows the district, to be kind enough to tell me that he will see to it that some means are taken whereby the licence may be cancelled. I do not know of any provincial government in Canada that would award a beer licence-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP THE SECRETARY OP STATE
speechtext: Who issues the licence?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP THE SECRETARY OP STATE
speechtext:
The United States government. No provincial government in Canada would dare to give a beer licence to a settlement of six Canadians near a United States community. That would not be done. It would be unfair and ridiculous. In this instance the profit is made not from selling beer to United States citizens, but from selling it to Canadians who cross the border. Of course they cannot bring the beer back with them, but they can drink as much of it as they like over there and, if they wish, they may get drunk.
Of course the granting of beer licences is left to the discretion of the governments concerned. In this instance it is just some bold action on the part of the authorities of Maine who have taken this action, just to laugh at the Canadian population. I hope the minister will see to this matter, and also that the case of Richard will be settled.
This case of Richard has been mentioned. It may be considered only a small matter, because it affects only a few animals-a herd of cattle and some horses-but there is a principle at stake. I do not see why United States customs officials may come boldly to

Canada, without reporting to the Canadian authorities, seize cattle and horses on the Canadian side, tie them to a fence on the United States side and then tell the farmer, "We will slaughter your animals within an hour if you do not pay the fine." That is very bold action.
I was shocked to receive a letter from Doctor Skelton informing me that he was instructed by the United States legation to tell me to get in direct touch with the United States authorities. The first time I spoke of the matter in the house I was very mild, but this time I am most indignant, when I see that no progress has been made. The other day the Department of External Affairs supplied me with a statement to the effect that I was fully informed of the facts. Surely I am. I am informed of this fact, that all that has been done by the Department of External Affairs is nothing; there has been some useless correspondence. We voted a tremendous amount of money, over a million dollars, for the Department of External Affairs, covering the Canadian legations throughout the world; and yet it is impossible to have a settlement in a small matter like this. If the department cannot settle such a small matter, what can they do among the nations of the world? It is by small actions that we judge great men. I am not mentioning any individual in particular, but I am sick of one of them who is considered a great man, and who is good for nothing. I take it as an insult, as a Canadian, to be told to get in touch, direct, with the United States authorities, when we have an enormous organization in the Department of External Affairs, one which becomes bigger and bigger all the time, and which has to do with the Canadian legations throughout the world.
We must have the pride of our nationality. We have lost a great deal of territory in Maine. On account of the rapacity of the people of the United States and the neglectfulness of English officials we have sacrificed our territory. We must have pride in our nation, and we must not be timid, even when dealing with a big nation like the United States. The rights of our nationals should be respected. In this instance I do not blame the government, but I do blame severely the officials of the Department of External Affairs because they have not taken proper action in this matter. I blame also the Canadian legation at Washington, where the minister is a non-entity-and I regret I have to say that. But it is my duty to defend the rights of my constituents. The Minister of Justice knows the affection I have for him. I have

Supply Bill
spoken to other members of the government without results. I am now asking him to be kind enough to help those good people, and the help given by him will never be forgotten.

I know the place, the situation and the people in whom my hon. friend is so deeply interested. The case of Ouellette had never occurred to me before. I find it strange, remembering conditions when I lived in that part of the country, to think that the state of Maine would give licences so that people from Canada could go there to drink. The situation was quite different in former days. However, I shall see that the matter is investigated, and if I can help in any way to prevent these abuses I shall be only too pleased to do so.
With respect to the second matter mentioned by the hon. member, concerning Mr. Richard, whom I know, I believe a hardship does arise. Mr. Richard's farm is situated partly in Canada and partly in the state of Maine. There is no division of any kind, and when his cattle go from Canada to Maine there is a violation of the laws of the United States- and vice versa. Some settlement has been effected, but of course it is not permanent. If I can be of any help to secure what the hon. member has in view I promise him I shall be happy to give it.

I believe-and it is said rather in praise of all members of the house-that the amount of work which has been done with the assistance of all hon. members within the past two weeks has been considerable, but nothing has been pressed unduly. The estimates of all the important departments have been carefully scrutinized. I admit that to-day some of the estimates were adopted rather speedily, but they are those of departments which are not usually contentious- the Department of the Secretary of State, the Department of Justice, the Department of Finance. The estimates of all the big departments have been passed after full consideration, and so far as I am concerned and so far as the government is concerned we were quite ready to grant more time for the purpose. However, I thank my hon. friend for his cooperation, and I am pleased to move that the committee rise, and report progress and ask leave to sit again.
May I ask the minister when we meet again? Is the house sitting to-night?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do
not see the necessity of sitting to-night. The work is almost finished. The bill which has been reported from the banking and commerce committee is being printed before being submitted to the house, and cannot be ready before to-morrow morning. To sit to-night just for the purpose of having the third reading of the budget bill does not seem to be warranted, and when the committee has reported I will move the adjournment of the house.
[Mr. Stewart.l
Why not have the third reading now?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It does
not matter.
Progress reported.
On motion of Mr. Lapointe (Quebec East) the house adjourned at 6.10 pan.
Friday, June 2, 1939
